raindrop._comment: Rain that lands. Kept apart from plain fall because a lifetime is what makes a drop land, and snow borrows fall and must not. Drops vary in speed, so a shared lifetime lands them across a wide band rather than along a waterline.

ripple._comment: Where a raindrop landed. Particles.png is a hollow ring, so a ripple is simply one of those spawned small and grown outward while it fades - which is what a ring on water does. It goes nowhere: its position is inherited from the drop that made it.

fall-drift._comment: A leaf turns over more lazily than a petal and swings wider doing it - it is bigger, flatter, and catches more air. It also keeps spinning in the picture plane while it does, which is the difference between a leaf falling and a leaf being dropped.

rise._comment: Horizontal wander stays a fraction of the climb, or the sparks read as wind. Vertical jitter stays well under speedY for the same reason - it subtracts from an upward speed, so a large one lets particles stall in mid-air.

wisp._comment: Appears in place rather than entering, rises a little, and is gone. Most of its life is spent fading, which is what makes it read as a wisp rather than a dot with a timer.

bubble._comment: Climbs a long way from the floor and pops at the end. The fade is quick where the wisp is slow, because a bubble bursting is an event and a wisp guttering out is not.

twinkle._comment: A star does not go anywhere; it sits and varies. Barely any speed at all, a long life so it stays put rather than shuffling the sky every few seconds, and a shallow pulse - a star that blinks out is a firefly.

streak._comment: A shooting star, and an event rather than weather - one or two on screen at a time, gone in under two seconds. Star_01A is drawn with its trail already running up-left, so the motion travels down-right at the matching angle and needs no lean of its own.

spark._comment: What a shooting star leaves behind where it burned out. It goes nowhere - its position is inherited from the streak that made it - and spends its whole short life swelling and fading.

firefly._comment: Blinks deeply but never all the way out, so one can be followed across the dark between flashes rather than lost and swapped for another. Lives in a patch of air rather than crossing the map - it appears, mills about for ten seconds or so, and is gone.

petal._comment: A petal falls the way a leaf does but turns over as it goes, edge-on and back, which is what a flat light thing does in air. Kept separate from fall-drift so the leaves keep the motion they were tuned with.

ray._comment: Shafts of light. They all lean the same way because they all come from one sun; the tilt is only enough to read as light through moving leaves. Most of a shaft life is spent fading, so the population breathes - one swells, holds, ebbs, and another opens somewhere else.

overcast._comment: Cloud shadows. Free to face any direction and to be pulled out of shape, because a cloud has no correct orientation and no correct proportions - and a screen of identically-oriented ones reads as a stamped sprite. Shallow queue compared to fog: there are few enough of these that most of them need to be on screen.

crawl._comment: Margin clears half a drawn sprite, so it tracks the scale the layers use. Jitter is a large share of the speed on purpose - fog drifting in lockstep reads as a sliding texture rather than as weather.

sounds._comment: Weather is a bed, not an event. It has to lose to an axe swing.

snow.description: Negative Peaks. Seeded from 'weather: light/moderate/heavy snow'.
snow._comment_sounds: Falling snow is silent. A whiteout is not - that noise is the wind driving it.

fog.description: Forest of Dreams. Seeded from 'weather: fog light/moderate/heavy' - identical but for density.

stops._comment: Small and many rather than few and huge. Fog is a field, and a field needs its particles to overlap into one another - a handful of screen-sized banks reads as a handful of banks, however faint each one is.
Density is per 816x624 of screen, not a particle count - the plugin scales it by area. These read as roughly 30/55/95 visible at 1080p.

embers.description: Volcanis Grotto. Seeded from 'WEATHER: fire and sparks'. Light_01C throughout - its whiteish-orange core reads as a spark; the Fire_ assets are whole fireballs and the Rain_ ones are droplets.

leaves.description: Outer Cliffs. Seeded from 'weather: leaves in the breeze'.
leaves._comment_sounds: The leaves are what the wind looks like, so the wind is what they sound like.

motes.description: Dim drifting lights in dark air. Seeded from 'weather: spirit darkness' - the most-used effect in the game, and every use of it is the Forlorn Basin.

submerged.description: Motes plus rising bubbles, for a flooded room. Seeded from 'weather: bubble darkness' - Passage 13.

clouds.description: NEW - not in CA today. Drifting cloud shadows for open sky. Untuned.

clear.description: Open sky with nothing in it. Shafts of light leaning across the world - warm from the sun, and the same shafts want a cooler tint under a moon.

sakura.description: NEW - not in CA today. Same motion as leaves, entirely different mood. Untuned.

stops._comment: Sakura_02A is a single petal and Sakura_01A is a whole blossom, so the petals are the weather and a very few intact flowers come down with them.

fireflies.description: NEW - not in CA today. Night-time forest. Light_01B tinted yellow-green, because a firefly is not a spirit-mote and the same asset serves both.

starfall.description: NEW - not in CA today. Clear night sky: a field of twinkles with the occasional streak through it. Star_03A is the twinkle and Star_01A is drawn already travelling down-right with its trail behind it; Star_02A is a solid yellow icon and belongs to no weather.

_comment_faces: The three below are not skies of their own - they are what 'clear' and 'breezy' wear in a
particular season. J-Weather-Time picks them by (type, season, phase) and hands the name
straight to layersFor, which is why they have to be real presets rather than overrides.

scorcher.description: NEW - the summer daytime face of a clear sky. Same shafts as 'clear' but pushed hot, with a slow warm shimmer rising through them. Light_01C is an orange core in a red glow, which is what heat looks like when it is standing still in the air.

frigid.description: NEW - the winter daytime face of a clear sky. A cold sun throws weaker, bluer shafts than a summer one, and the air itself glitters: on a still freezing day the moisture in it hangs as suspended ice rather than falling. That is what the twinkling snowflakes are - diamond dust, not snowfall.

maple.description: NEW - the autumn face of a breeze. The same motions as 'leaves' wearing a different tree. Leaf_03C is already painted red and Leaf_03B is the unturned green one, so a heavy wind carries both; Leaf_03A is the same shape in grey and takes an amber tint. These are 210px where Leaf_04A is 31px, which is the whole reason the scales look so different from the preset this was copied from.
maple._comment_sounds: Autumn wind is still wind, so this borrows the leaves ladder unchanged.

_comment_ids: These are what get written into game variables, so events can branch on the weather.
They are declared rather than derived from position on purpose: if they were positional,
inserting a preset above another would silently renumber it and every conditional branch
already written against the old number would quietly start meaning something else.
Add new presets with new numbers. Never renumber an existing one.
_comment_sky: Everything below belongs to J-Weather-Time. J-Weather itself never reads it.
A TYPE is a condition the sky walks between. A FACE is the preset that type is drawn with at a
given season and hour - a clear summer afternoon and a clear winter afternoon are one state and
two completely different pictures, and folding that into the graph would double every edge.
Transition weights are relative and need not sum to anything. Seasons hard-gate which types are
possible at all, because 'it never snows in summer' is a fact about the world where a weight of
zero is only a fact about dice.

clear._comment: Order matters - the first rule whose keys all match wins, so the summer night rule must sit above the general night rule.

breezy._comment: In autumn all wind is maple wind - there is no plain leaf breeze between months 9 and 11, deliberately.

mist._comment: Caps at moderate on purpose: a heavy mist is just fog, and fog is a place rather than a sky.

monsoon._comment: A separate type rather than 'rain at heavy' so the strength drift cannot argue it down.

spring._comment: Mild and showery. Sakura is the season's signature and reachable only from calm weather.

summer._comment: Clear-biased and dry. Rain when it comes arrives through overcast and leaves the same way.

autumn._comment: Windy and wet. A monsoon can only be entered from rain and can only leave back into it, which is what keeps it an event rather than a mood.

winter._comment: Cold. Snow is reachable from everywhere because the Negative Peaks should not have to wait three phases for it.

_comment_months: A season says what is POSSIBLE. A month says what is LIKELY, within that.
Each number multiplies that condition's weight while rolling into it, so 1 is 'leave the
graph alone', 4 is 'four times as wanted as authored', and 0 is 'not this month'. A month
names only the conditions it has an opinion about.
This is what makes sakura a fortnight in April rather than a whole spring, August the
uncomfortable stretch, October the monsoon month, and the deep snow December and January
with February visibly letting go of it.
Zero is safe and is how sakura ENDS rather than fades - a sky still blossoming on the last
day of month 4 steps straight out of it on the next phase. What is not safe is zeroing
every exit from one condition; config validation reports that at boot.
_comment_voices: What somebody travelling with you says about the weather, on the 'Right Now' view.
Keyed by PRESET, then optionally by strength. A preset that writes only 'any' uses those
lines whatever the strength is, so you owe fifteen states rather than forty-five - split a
preset into light/moderate/heavy only where a drizzle and a downpour want different words.
'none' covers standing somewhere with no weather at all.
'who' is an ACTOR ID. The name and the face both come from the database, so renaming
somebody in the editor renames them here - and only actors currently in the party are ever
picked, so nobody remarks on the weather before you have met them. Jerald is 1, Rupert 2.
One line is chosen at random each time the view is opened. Write at least two per state or
it stops feeling like a person and starts feeling like a tooltip.
EVERYTHING BELOW IS PLACEHOLDER, written to prove the mechanism. Replace it.

any.says: Nothing coming down in here. Small mercies.
Dry, at least. I'll take dry.
Wet one. Hope you packed something that dries fast.
It's raining. I have opinions about that, none of them good.

heavy.says: This is less rain and more the sky emptying itself.
I can't see ten paces. Whatever we're doing, let's do it tomorrow.

any.says: Not a thing up there. Good day to be going somewhere.
Clear as anything. Enjoy it, it never lasts.
It is absolutely cooking out here. Drink something.
I am going to melt. I want that noted.
Snow's coming down. Watch your footing up high.
Cold. Wet. Cold and wet. Wonderful.
Whole sky's awake tonight. Worth stopping for a minute.
You don't get skies like this in a city. That's the one thing.

_comment_places: The destinations the DIAGNOSTIC forecast reports on - the one behind the showDebugForecast
plugin command, not anything a player sees. Naming places in a player-facing screen would
tell them the Negative Peaks exist before they have found them.
A place is a NAME and a MAP ID and nothing else. The forecast reads that map's own note off
disk and runs it through the same resolver the game uses on arrival, so retagging a map
updates the forecast and the two can never disagree. Nothing about a place's weather is
Rows appear in the order listed. A map id that does not exist is reported and dropped.

_comment_climates: A climate is how one KIND OF PLACE answers the sky rather than following it. It only bends a
look the map already authored with <weather:...>; a map with no weather of its own follows the
sky directly and a climate tag on it does nothing.
byType and byIntensity are alternatives, not layers - declare one. `default` is the fallback for

dreaming._comment: Forest of Dreams. The fog thickens as the sky clears, which is the one thing a map tag cannot say.
